claim: Shifting attention among visual stimuli at different locations modulates neuronal responses in heterogeneous ways, depending on where those stimuli lie within the receptive fields of neurons.
source: Shifting attention among visual stimuli at different locations modulates neuronal responses in heterogeneous ways, depending on where those stimuli lie within the receptive fields of neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention modulation that is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Attention interacts uniformly with the spatially-varying excitation and suppression associated with the receptive field.
source: We found that attention interacts uniformly with the spatially-varying excitation and suppression associated with the receptive field.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between attention and spatially-varying excitation and suppression explained the large variability in attention modulation across neurons.
source: This interaction explained the large variability in attention modulation across neurons, and a non-additive relationship among stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention modulation that has not been previously described.
evidence: This is a finding derived from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: There is a non-additive relationship among stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention modulation.
source: This interaction explained the large variability in attention modulation across neurons, and a non-additive relationship among stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention modulation that has not been previously described.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A spatially-tuned normalization model precisely accounted for all observed attention modulations and for the spatial summation properties of neurons.
source: A spatially-tuned normalization model precisely accounted for all observed attention modulations and for the spatial summation properties of neurons.
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: Spatial attention sifts through visual stimuli, enhancing perception at behaviorally-relevant locations.
source: Spatial attention sifts through the plethora of stimuli – enhancing perception at behaviorally-relevant locations – but the underlying neural principles of this process are not fully understood (Chun et al., 2011; Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000; Posner, 1980; Carrasco, 2011; Roelfsema et al., 1998; Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neuronal responses modulate as attention shifts among stimuli at different receptive-field locations.
source: Neuronal responses modulate as attention shifts among stimuli at different receptive-field locations (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Treue and Maunsell, 1996; Reynolds et al., 1999; Martínez-Trujillo and Treue, 2002; Ghose and Maunsell, 2008; Lee and Maunsell, 2010; Ni et al., 2012; Recanzone and Wurtz, 2000; Luck et al., 1997; Motter, 1993; Chelazzi et al., 1998; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Depending on the stimulus configuration, attending to a non-preferred stimulus can either increase or suppress activity.
source: For example, depending on the stimulus configuration, attending to a non-preferred stimulus can either increase or suppress activity (e.g. Treue and Maunsell, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Normalization models of attention provide a succinct framework in which complex response modulations can be understood.
source: Normalization models of attention provide a succinct framework in which these complex response modulations can be understood (Reynolds et al., 1999; Ghose, 2009; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Lee, 2009; Boynton, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Only a few studies have directly tested normalization models of attention against the responses of individual neurons to various stimulus configurations.
source: However, only a few studies have directly tested these models against the responses of individual neurons to various stimulus configurations (Ni et al., 2012; Lee, 2009; Sanayei et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Normalization models of attention assume that attention acts on stimulus-induced excitation and suppression to modulate neuronal responses.
source: Normalization models of attention assume that attention acts on stimulus-induced excitation and suppression to modulate neuronal responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions of normalization models.

claim: Both excitation and suppression vary spatially within the receptive field: excitation is largely restricted to the classical receptive field (cRF), while suppression extends far beyond into the surround.
source: Importantly, both excitation and suppression vary spatially within the receptive field: excitation is largely restricted to the classical receptive field (cRF), while suppression extends far beyond into the surround (Cavanaugh et al., 2002a, 2002b; Sceniak et al., 1999; Desimone and Schein, 1987; Carandini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: How attention interacts with the receptive field structure of neurons remains unclear.
source: Crucially, how attention interacts with the receptive field structure of neurons remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The way that attention acts on neuronal responses when shifted among stimuli inside the cRF versus when shifted to stimuli inside the surround has not been compared directly.
source: For example, the way that attention acts on neuronal responses when shifted among stimuli inside the cRF versus when shifted to stimuli inside the surround has not been compared directly (Motter, 1993; Sanayei et al., 2015; Sundberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Feedforward-, feedback- and intracortical circuitries are thought to contribute differentially to the suppressive and excitatory inputs associated with stimuli in either the cRF or the surround.
source: Differences may occur because feedforward-, feedback- and intracortical circuitries are thought to contribute differentially to the suppressive and excitatory inputs associated with stimuli in either the cRF or the surround (Angelucci et al., 2014), and because the cRF and the surround presumably serve different functional roles (Angelucci et al., 2014; Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The cRF and the surround presumably serve different functional roles.
source: Differences may occur because feedforward-, feedback- and intracortical circuitries are thought to contribute differentially to the suppressive and excitatory inputs associated with stimuli in either the cRF or the surround (Angelucci et al., 2014), and because the cRF and the surround presumably serve different functional roles (Angelucci et al., 2014; Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The interaction between attention and the receptive field structure determines which neurons are most affected by attention and consequently are most likely to influence attentional behavior.
source: This is a pivotal open question because, as we will show below, the interaction between attention and the receptive field structure determines which neurons are most affected by attention and consequently are most likely to influence attentional behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the study's findings.

claim: The principles that drive attention modulation are remarkably similar within the classical receptive field and the surround.
source: We find that the principles that drive attention modulation are remarkably similar within the classical receptive field and the surround.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Stimuli induce excitation and suppression that varies spatially.
source: We show that stimuli induce excitation and suppression that varies spatially, and that attention interacts with this spatially-varying excitation and suppression.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Attention interacts with spatially-varying excitation and suppression.
source: We show that stimuli induce excitation and suppression that varies spatially, and that attention interacts with this spatially-varying excitation and suppression.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The spatially-tuned normalization model, wherein attention multiplies both the excitatory and spatially-varying normalization term, precisely accounted for all neuronal responses to either single or multiple stimuli, either attended or unattended, presented inside either the cRF or the surround.
source: A spatially-tuned normalization model, wherein attention multiplies both the excitatory and spatially-varying normalization term, precisely accounted for all neuronal responses to either single or multiple stimuli, either attended or unattended, presented inside either the cRF or the surround.
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: The model relates stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention-related modulation to each other.
source: The model relates stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention-related modulation to each other, and unifies spatial summation and attention-related modulation across different regions of the receptive field.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities.

claim: The model unifies spatial summation and attention-related modulation across different regions of the receptive field.
source: The model relates stimulus selectivity, stimulus-induced suppression and attention-related modulation to each other, and unifies spatial summation and attention-related modulation across different regions of the receptive field.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities.

claim: Targets were much more likely detected at a cued location than at an uncued location.
source: The attention cue considerably affected behavioral performance in the task: targets were much more likely detected at a cued location than at an uncued location, even when the uncued location was adjacent to the cued location (Figure 1B,C; valid vs. invalid near: monkey M1: p=8 × 10−27, M2: p=1 × 10−26; valid vs. invalid far: M1: p=1 × 10−36, M2: p=2 × 10−58; paired t-test on the average proportion correct across sessions; M1: N = 52; M2: N = 78).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the task, shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The improved performance indicates that the monkeys preferentially attended to the cued stimulus location.
source: The improved performance indicates that the monkeys preferentially attended to the cued stimulus location, which allowed us to compare neuronal responses among conditions in which attention was directed to different stimulus locations within neurons' cRF or surround.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: 728 neurons were recorded in visual area V4 in the left hemisphere of two monkeys.
source: We recorded from 728 neurons in visual area V4 in the left hemisphere of two monkeys (monkey M1: 264; M2: 464) while they performed the visual-detection task in which spatial attention was controlled.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: All results presented are based on the activity of 728 single neurons.
source: All results presented here are based on the activity of these 728 single neurons, but all findings were confirmed in the responses of 12,067 multi-unit clusters (M1: 4709; M2: 7358).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analyses.

claim: All findings were confirmed in the responses of 12,067 multi-unit clusters.
source: All results presented here are based on the activity of these 728 single neurons, but all findings were confirmed in the responses of 12,067 multi-unit clusters (M1: 4709; M2: 7358).
evidence: This is a description of the data used to confirm the findings.

claim: Neurons' receptive field centers were located in the lower right visual field.
source: The neurons' receptive field centers were located in the lower right visual field (black dots in Figure 2A for an example session).
evidence: This is based on receptive field mapping data, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Shifting attention between two Gabors inside the cRF was associated with larger response changes for neurons with more selective responses to the component Gabors of the Gabor pair.
source: Shifting attention between two Gabors inside the cRF was associated with larger response changes for neurons with more selective responses to the component Gabors of the Gabor pair (Figure 4A; cRF-cRF configuration; p=4 × 10−109 for a non-zero slope; linear regression) (Reynolds et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Attention-related modulation was stronger for neurons that responded more selectively to the cRF and surround stimulus.
source: Attention-related modulation was also stronger for neurons that responded more selectively to the cRF and surround stimulus (Figure 4B; sRF-cRF configuration; p=3 × 10−76 for a non-zero slope; linear regression).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Attention-related modulation increases more with selectivity in the cRF-cRF than in the sRF-cRF configuration.
source: Comparing Figure 4A and B shows that attention-related modulation increases more with selectivity in the cRF-cRF than in the sRF-cRF configuration (p=5 × 10−4 for different slopes in each receptive-field configuration; general linear model).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of the data in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: V4 neuronal responses on average decrease when a non-preferred stimulus is added to a preferred stimulus inside their cRF.
source: V4 neuronal responses on average decrease when a non-preferred stimulus is added to a preferred stimulus inside their cRF (Figure 4C; average suppression index = 0.08, p=4 × 10−104; t-test for a difference from zero) (Reynolds et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Stimulating the surround decreases the average responses of V4 neurons.
source: Similarly, stimulating the surround decreases the average responses of V4 neurons (Figure 4D; average suppression index = 0.04, p=2 × 10−28; t-test) (Schein and Desimone, 1990).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Stimuli inside the surround suppressed the neuronal responses less than stimuli inside the cRF.
source: However, stimuli inside the surround suppressed the neuronal responses less than stimuli inside the cRF: the average suppression index for the surround condition (sRF-cRF) was significantly smaller than the average suppression index for the cRF condition (M1: p=9 × 10−6; M2: p=4 × 10−15; t-test; see below and Figure 7 for further discussion).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of the experimental data.

claim: V4 neurons with stronger stimulus-induced suppression by cRF stimuli also showed stronger attention modulation.
source: Extending previous findings in area MT (Ni et al., 2012; Lee, 2009), we find that V4 neurons with stronger stimulus-induced suppression by cRF stimuli also showed stronger attention modulation (Figure 4E; p=1 × 10−31 for a non-zero slope; linear regression).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Attention modulation was stronger for neurons whose responses were more suppressed by a surround stimulus.
source: Furthermore, and consistent with a previous study (Sundberg et al., 2009), attention modulation was also stronger for neurons whose responses were more suppressed by a surround stimulus (Figure 4F; p=5 × 10−4 for a non-zero slope; linear regression).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Attention-related modulation increases more with stimulus-induced suppression in the sRF-cRF than in the cRF-cRF configuration.
source: However, comparing Figure 4E and F shows that attention-related modulation increases more with stimulus-induced suppression in the sRF-cRF than in the cRF-cRF configuration (p=0.005 for different slopes in each receptive-field configuration; general linear model).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of the data in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression were not significantly correlated with each other across neurons.
source: In the present study, however, stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression were not significantly correlated with each other across neurons (Figure 4G,H Pearson correlation = 0.02, p=0.32; see Discussion for further comments on the difference between studies).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: The correlations between stimulus selectivity and attention modulation, and that between stimulus-induced suppression and attention modulation, are not explained by an underlying correlation between selectivity and suppression.
source: This finding shows that the correlations between stimulus selectivity and attention modulation, and that between stimulus-induced suppression and attention modulation, are not explained by an underlying correlation between selectivity and suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between selectivity and suppression.

claim: For both receptive-field configurations, the relationship between attention modulation, selectivity, and stimulus-induced suppression is non-additive.
source: Figure 5 shows how attention modulation varies with selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression (5A; cRF-cRF, 5B; sRF-cRF). For both configurations, the relationship is non-additive.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: When stimulus-induced suppression is low, attention modulation will be weak, even when attention is shifted between a strong and a weak stimulus.
source: Specifically, Figure 5A and B show that when stimulus-induced suppression is low, attention modulation will be weak, even when attention is shifted between a strong and a weak stimulus (upper left corner in Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The effect of selectivity near zero stimulus-induced suppression is weak, although significant.
source: That is, the plots show that the effect of selectivity near zero stimulus-induced suppression is weak, although significant (main effect of selectivity at zero stimulus-induced suppression: cRF-cRF: p=2 × 10−64; sRF-cRF: p=2 × 10−60; M1: p=7 × 10−136 across RF configurations; M2: p=5 × 10−30 across RF configurations).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: When selectivity is low, attention modulation will be weak, even when attention is shifted between stimuli that strongly suppress each other's response.
source: Conversely, when selectivity is low, attention modulation will also be weak, even when attention is shifted between stimuli that strongly suppress each other's response (bottom right corner in Figure 5A,B; effect of stimulus-induced suppression at zero selectivity: cRF-cRF: p=0.5; sRF-cRF: p=0.6; M1: p=0.4 across RF configurations; M2: p=0.3 across RF configurations).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Strong attention-related modulation occurs only when selectivity and suppression are both large, and this was true for both RF configurations.
source: Strong attention-related modulation occurs only when selectivity and suppression are both large, and this was true for both RF configurations (upper right corner in Figure 5A,B; interaction between stimulus-induced suppression and selectivity: cRF-cRF: p=2 × 10−9; sRF-cRF: p=3 × 10−6; M1: p=1 × 10−4 across RF configurations; M2: p=3 × 10−20 across RF configurations).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The interaction between selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression did not differ significantly between the cRF-cRF and sRF-cRF configuration.
source: The interaction between selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression did not differ significantly between the cRF-cRF and sRF-cRF configuration (M1: p=0.6; M2: p=0.85; 3-way interaction), nor did any other interaction with RF configuration.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The observed data are 347 times more likely to agree with a regression model that does not distinguish between the cRF-cRF and sRF-cRF configurations than with a model that does include RF-configuration as a predictor.
source: This analysis showed that the observed data are 347 times more likely to agree with a regression model that does not distinguish between the cRF-cRF and sRF-cRF configurations than with a model that does include RF-configuration as a predictor.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Attention modulation is driven by similar mechanisms within the cRF and the surround.
source: Thus attention modulation is driven by similar mechanisms within the cRF and the surround.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses.

claim: When attention shifted between stimuli at two approximately-equally responsive cRF positions, similar effects were observed as with unequally-responsive positions.
source: When attention shifted between stimuli at two approximately-equally responsive cRF positions (less than 2 spike/s response difference when each of two cRF positions is stimulated with an identical single stimulus), similar effects were observed (main effect of orientation selectivity: p<0.001; main effect suppression: p=0.7; interaction between feature selectivity and suppression: p=0.02; multiple linear regression).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a subset of the experimental data.

claim: All findings were replicated using only the data obtained with Gabor pairs consisting of identical Gabors.
source: All of the above findings were replicated using only the data obtained with Gabor pairs consisting of identical Gabors (main effect spatial selectivity: p=4 × 10−22; main effect suppression: p=0.29; interaction between spatial selectivity and suppression: p=6 × 10−6; multiple linear regression).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a subset of the experimental data.

claim: Attention-related modulation depends on a differential response to the component stimuli of a compound stimulus, regardless of the origin of the response difference (feature or spatial).
source: This indicates that attention-related modulation depends on a differential response to the component stimuli of a compound stimulus, regardless of the origin of the response difference (feature or spatial).
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of different stimulus conditions.

claim: The spatially-tuned normalization model provided an accurate account of the neuronal data, giving a median two-fold cross-validated explained variance of 87% across neurons.
source: The spatially-tuned normalization model provided an accurate account of the neuronal data, giving a median two-fold cross-validated explained variance of 87% across neurons (M1: 86%; M2: 88%).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: For the 309 neurons that were tested in both a cRF-cRF and an sRF-cRF configuration the responses were equally well explained.
source: For the 309 neurons (M1: 97; M2: 212) that were tested in both a cRF-cRF and an sRF-cRF configuration the responses were equally well explained (M1: 86%; M2: 87%).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: The model captures the way attention modulates neuronal responses to stimuli inside the cRF or the surround.
source: The model captures the way attention modulates neuronal responses to stimuli inside the cRF or the surround.
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: The model reproduces the way stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression interacted in both the cRF-cRF and the sRF-cRF configurations.
source: The model reproduces the way stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression interacted in both the cRF-cRF and the sRF-cRF configurations: predicting large attention modulation when both selectivity and suppression are strong, but little attention modulation when either selectivity or suppression is low.
evidence: This is based on model predictions compared to experimental data.

claim: The model accounts for the neuronal effects of attention to single stimuli at different receptive field locations.
source: Importantly, the model also accounts for the neuronal effects of attention to single stimuli at different receptive field locations.
evidence: This is based on model predictions compared to experimental data.

claim: Attention modulation to single stimuli is typically small compared to attention modulation with multiple stimuli.
source: Attention modulation to single stimuli is typically small compared to attention modulation with multiple stimuli.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In single stimulus conditions there are no suppressive influences from a flanking stimulus, and these suppressive influences are necessary to induce strong attention modulation.
source: This is because in single stimulus conditions there are no suppressive influences from a flanking stimulus, and we have shown that these suppressive influences are necessary to induce strong attention modulation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Within neurons, locations closest to the receptive-field center induced on average greater suppression than locations furthest away from the receptive-field center.
source: Within neurons, locations closest to the receptive-field center induced on average greater suppression than locations furthest away from the receptive-field center (average α-parameter values of closest vs. furthest location: p=2 × 10−23; M1: p=7 × 10−5; M2: p=0.005; paired permutation t-test).
evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameters fitted to the experimental data.

claim: Lower α-values at greater distances are consistent with the observation that surround suppression is significantly weaker than cRF suppression.
source: Lower α-values at greater distances are consistent with the observation that surround suppression is significantly weaker than cRF suppression (Figure 4C,D; see above).
evidence: This is an inference from the model parameters and experimental data.

claim: The receptive field structure of V4 neurons is similar to that previously observed in primary visual cortex (V1): both excitation and suppression are maximal near the receptive-field center, but excitation is more spatially concentrated, with suppression stretching over larger distances.
source: Comparing the curves for the excitatory (black) and the suppressive drive (gray) reveals a striking similarity between the receptive field structure of V4 neurons and that previously observed in primary visual cortex (V1) (Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Sceniak et al., 1999; DeAngelis et al., 1994): both excitation and suppression are maximal near the receptive-field center, but excitation is more spatially concentrated, with suppression stretching over larger distances.
evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameters fitted to the experimental data, compared to prior work.

claim: The spatial pattern of suppression suggests that suppression in the cRF and the surround are continuous extensions of one another.
source: The spatial pattern of suppression suggests that suppression in the cRF and the surround are continuous extensions of one another.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of model parameters.

claim: Attention operates uniformly on the spatially-continuous excitation and suppression of a neuron's receptive field.
source: These findings indicate that attention operates uniformly on the spatially-continuous excitation and suppression of a neuron's receptive field.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: A constrained model with fixed attention parameter β accounted almost as well for the data as the model in which β was free to vary.
source: We fixed the attention parameter β at a constant value for all neurons, i.e. as the mean β value across neurons when estimated as a free parameter. This constrained model accounted almost as well for the data as the model in which β was free to vary (median two-fold cross-validated percentage explained variance 86%, compared to 87% for the unconstrained model).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: Differences in attention modulation between neurons are only weakly related to differences in the top-down attention signal across neurons.
source: This finding suggests that differences in attention modulation between neurons are only weakly related to differences in the top-down attention signal across neurons (see also [Ni et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results.

claim: When the α terms were kept constant and β was allowed to vary across neurons, the model's performance decreased significantly.
source: In contrast, spatial tuning is important. When we instead kept the α terms constant and allowed β to vary across neurons, the model's performance decreased significantly (77%; p=0.004, Sequential F-test), especially for neurons that were tested in both a cRF-cRF and an sRF-cRF configuration (73%; p=0.002).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: When a fixed stimulus is shown, differences in attention modulation across neurons appear to arise when a relatively uniform top-down attention signal interacts with the different amounts of excitation and suppression elicited by that stimulus in each neuron.
source: Hence when a fixed stimulus is shown, differences in attention modulation across neurons appear to arise when a relatively uniform top-down attention signal interacts with the different amounts of excitation and suppression elicited by that stimulus in each neuron.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results.

claim: Reynolds et al. (1999) observed a strong correlation between stimulus selectivity and their index of stimulus-induced suppression.
source: Reynolds et al. (1999) observed a strong correlation between stimulus selectivity and their index of stimulus-induced suppression.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work.

claim: The strong correlation observed by Reynolds et al. is not a general property of spatial summation in visual cortex.
source: It is important to note that this strong correlation is not a general property of spatial summation in visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of the current study with prior work.

claim: The correlation observed by Reynolds et al. likely arose from the experimental design used in that study.
source: Instead, the correlation they observed likely arose from the experimental design used in that study.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of the current study with prior work.

claim: Varying the orientation and color of a stimulus, but not its location, varies predominantly the excitation and not the suppression to the neuron.
source: But varying the orientation and color of a stimulus, but not its location, varies predominantly the excitation and not the suppression to the neuron (see Appendix; we found no evidence for orientation-tuned suppression in our data).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Under more general stimulus conditions wherein stimuli can fall on any receptive field location, stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression are not correlated.
source: Hence, under more general stimulus conditions wherein stimuli can fall on any receptive field location, stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression are not correlated.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Shifting attention between a strong and a weak stimulus changes which neuronal inputs are emphasized, thereby causing neuronal-response modulations.
source: Shifting attention between a strong and a weak stimulus, each presented at different receptive-field locations, changes which neuronal inputs are emphasized, thereby causing neuronal-response modulations.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention mechanisms.

claim: Clear-cut differential processing only occurs if the weaker stimulus also induces strong suppression: without suppression, attention has no leverage to amplify input differences.
source: However, we show that such clear-cut differential processing only occurs if the weaker stimulus also induces strong suppression: without suppression, attention has no leverage to amplify input differences.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: Neither Sundberg et al. (2009) nor Sanayei et al. (2015) used a condition with both stimuli positioned inside the cRF (cRF-cRF).
source: Both Sundberg et al. (2009) and Sanayei et al. (2015) used conditions with one stimulus inside the classical receptive field and at least one other stimulus in the surround (sRF-cRF). However, neither of these studies used a condition with both stimuli positioned inside the cRF (cRF-cRF).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work.

claim: A direct comparison of attention modulation within the cRF and the surround could not be performed in the studies by Sundberg et al. (2009) and Sanayei et al. (2015).
source: Hence, a direct comparison of attention modulation within the cRF and the surround could not be performed in these studies.
evidence: This is an inference from the description of prior work.

claim: Seeing the similarity between attentional effects in both receptive field regions requires examination of the combined relationship, i.e. interaction, between attention modulation and both stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression.
source: Importantly, we found that seeing the similarity between attentional effects in both receptive field regions requires examination of the combined relationship, i.e. interaction, between attention modulation and both stimulus selectivity and stimulus-induced suppression (Figure 4 versus 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Sanayei et al. never measured the neuronal effects of attention when attention was directed to the surround stimulus.
source: Sanayei et al. fit different (normalization) models, but never measured the neuronal effects of attention when attention was directed to the surround stimulus; the authors only compared the effects of attention to the cRF stimulus, with or without surround stimulation, versus attention to a distant stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work.

claim: Sanayei et al. lacked the crucial information needed to examine how surround suppression affects attention modulation and to test the efficacy of normalization models.
source: Thus, Sanayei et al. lacked the crucial information needed to examine how surround suppression affects attention modulation and to test the efficacy of normalization models.
evidence: This is an inference from the description of prior work.

claim: The good fits of the spatially-tuned normalization model to the data obtained in both receptive field configurations provided further evidence that attention acts similarly inside the cRF and the surround.
source: The good fits of the spatially-tuned normalization model to the data obtained in both receptive field configurations provided further evidence that attention acts similarly inside the cRF and the surround.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results.

claim: Suppression and excitation may rely on distinct mechanisms in different regions of the receptive field.
source: Suppression and excitation may rely on distinct mechanisms in different regions of the receptive field (Angelucci et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The way attention interacts with excitation and suppression across different regions of the receptive field is remarkably similar.
source: Nonetheless, our findings show that the way attention interacts with excitation and suppression across different regions of the receptive field is remarkably similar.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: Two of the more elaborate normalization models of attention explicitly assumed that attention acts on a specific receptive-field structure, namely one that encompasses a relatively narrow excitatory field in addition to a wider suppressive field.
source: Two of the more elaborate models explicitly assumed that attention acts on a specific receptive-field structure, namely one that encompasses a relatively narrow excitatory field in addition to a wider suppressive field (Ghose, 2009; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work.

claim: This receptive-field structure is based on findings from primary visual cortex (V1).
source: This receptive-field structure is based on findings from primary visual cortex (V1) (Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Sceniak et al., 1999; DeAngelis et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: None of the prior studies empirically tested if attention actually operates on the spatially-varying excitation and suppression implied by such a receptive field structure.
source: It is important to note, however, that none of these studies empirically tested if attention actually operates on the spatially-varying excitation and suppression implied by such a receptive field structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in prior work.

claim: The spatially-tuned normalization model used in this study made no assumptions about the structure of excitation and suppression in the receptive field of V4 neurons.
source: We started with a spatially-tuned normalization model that made no assumptions about the structure of excitation and suppression in the receptive field of V4 neurons.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The naive model reveals that the receptive field organization of V4 neurons strongly resembles that of V1 neurons.
source: Interestingly, this naive model reveals that the receptive field organization of V4 neurons strongly resembles that of V1 neurons (Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Sceniak et al., 1999; DeAngelis et al., 1994): both excitation and suppression are maximal near the receptive-field center, but excitation is more spatially concentrated, while suppression stretches over larger distances.
evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameters fitted to the experimental data, compared to prior work.

claim: Similar receptive field organizations can be found throughout different stages of visual cortex.
source: These findings suggest that similar receptive field organizations can be found throughout different stages of visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of V4 and V1 receptive field structures.

claim: Attention operates uniformly across the spatially-varying excitation and suppression of a receptive field: throughout the receptive field, including the surround, attention-related modulations of neuronal responses is governed by very similar normalization rules.
source: Importantly, our findings show that attention operates uniformly across the spatially-varying excitation and suppression of a receptive field: throughout the receptive field, including the surround, attention-related modulations of neuronal responses is governed by very similar normalization rules.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: The finding that the rules of neuronal attention modulation are similar across different regions of the receptive field simplifies our view of attentional operations in visual cortex.
source: The finding that the rules of neuronal attention modulation are similar across different regions of the receptive field simplifies our view of attentional operations in visual cortex, and provides strong support for normalization models of attention (Ghose, 2009; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The origin of the stimulus-induced excitation is not important for determining the magnitude of attention modulation: there is no distinction between excitation related to a neuron's feature tuning (i.e. orientation tuning) or spatial tuning (i.e. receptive field).
source: We also show that the origin of the stimulus-induced excitation is not important for determining the magnitude of attention modulation: we found no distinction between excitation related to a neuron's feature tuning (i.e. orientation tuning) or spatial tuning (i.e. receptive field).
evidence: This is based on analysis of different stimulus conditions.

claim: What matters for neuronal attention modulation is stimulus-induced excitation, regardless of its origin, in conjunction with spatially-tuned suppression.
source: What matters for neuronal attention modulation is stimulus-induced excitation, regardless of its origin, in conjunction with spatially-tuned suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: When a particular stimulus configuration induces variable amounts of excitation and suppression in different neurons, attention-related modulations will vary across these neurons.
source: It follows that when a particular stimulus configuration induces variable amounts of excitation and suppression in different neurons, attention-related modulations will vary across these neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The fact that attention operates on the spatially-varying excitation and suppression of a receptive field determines which neurons will be most influenced by attention.
source: The fact that attention operates on the spatially-varying excitation and suppression of a receptive field has important implications, as it determines which neurons will be most influenced by attention.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: With a given number of stimuli presented inside the receptive field, attention to a preferred stimulus shown inside the center of the receptive field typically has the greatest potential to elevate neuronal responses.
source: For instance, with a given number of stimuli presented inside the receptive field, attention to a preferred stimulus shown inside the center of the receptive field typically has the greatest potential to elevate neuronal responses.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings and model.

claim: Stimuli near the receptive field center generally elicit most excitation and are most likely to induce the greatest suppression.
source: This is true not only because stimuli near the receptive field center generally elicit most excitation, but also because such stimuli are most likely to induce the greatest suppression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameters fitted to the experimental data.

claim: The elevated suppression by center stimuli gives them more weight in normalization mechanisms as it allows them to better discount the suppressive influences from other simultaneously presented stimuli.
source: The elevated suppression by center stimuli gives them more weight in normalization mechanisms as it allows them to better discount the suppressive influences from other simultaneously presented stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and experimental data.

claim: Attention to a weak stimulus inside the receptive field center will in general reduce responses more than attention to a weak stimulus elsewhere in the receptive field, including the surround.
source: Similarly, attention to a weak stimulus inside the receptive field center will in general reduce responses more than attention to a weak stimulus elsewhere in the receptive field, including the surround.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and experimental data.

claim: Because the surround is so much larger than the cRF it can contribute considerable suppression.
source: Indeed, because the surround is so much larger than the cRF it can contribute considerable suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from the receptive field structure.

claim: Strong surround suppression likely occurs under natural viewing conditions where stimuli are shown throughout the visual field, many of them covering the surround.
source: Such strong surround suppression likely occurs under natural viewing conditions where stimuli are shown throughout the visual field, many of them covering the surround (Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Ozeki et al., 2009; Haider et al., 2010; Coen-Cagli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The normalization model predicts that strong surround suppression may robustly amplify attention modulation, much beyond the attention modulation observed without surround suppression.
source: The normalization model predicts that such strong surround suppression may robustly amplify attention modulation, much beyond the attention modulation observed without surround suppression.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Model neurons with a surround strongly modulated their responses by attention, but those without a surround much less.
source: The model neurons with a surround strongly modulated their responses by attention, but those without a surround much less (Figure 8F upper vs. lower panel).
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 8.

claim: An important contribution of the surround may lie in its ability to amplify attention-related response modulations.
source: Hence, although the precise role of the surround is still unknown (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Sachdev et al., 2012), an important contribution of the surround may lie in its ability to amplify attention-related response modulations.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations and experimental data.
